title: Health outcomes associated with calcium antagonists compared with other first-line antihypertensive therapies: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
authors: Pahor M, Psaty BM, Alderman MH, Applegate WB, Williamson JD, Cavazzini C, et al.
followUp: trials with at least 2 years of follow-up
population: Nine randomised trials in hypertension with at least 100 patients assigned intermediate-acting or long-acting calcium antagonists (n=12,699) or diuretics, beta blockers, ACE inhibitors or clonidine (n=15,044)
funder: not read: the archived publisher page shows only the summary and the full text requires a subscription.
result: With similar control of systolic and diastolic pressure, calcium antagonists against other drugs gave higher risks of acute myocardial infarction (odds ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.43), congestive heart failure (1.25, 1.07 to 1.46) and major cardiovascular events (1.10, 1.02 to 1.18); differences in stroke (0.90, 0.80 to 1.02) and all-cause mortality (1.03, 0.94 to 1.13) were within chance. The authors concluded that longer-acting calcium antagonists could not be recommended as first-line therapy for hypertension.
